newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's patriarch slams poverty, wage arrears.
newsitem.headline: Russia's patriarch slams poverty, wage arrears.

text.p: The head of the Russian Orthodox church, Patriarch Alexiy II, appealed to the Kremlin on Monday, Christmas Eve in the Orthodox calendar, to remember Russia's poor and tackle the problem of unpaid wages and pensions.

"We urge the leadership of the country...and all those responsible for the non-payment of pensions, wages and student grants to recognise the urgent need for resolution of this problem," he said in an address carried by the Moskovsky Komsomolets newspaper.

President Boris Yeltsin has pledged urgent action to clear the huge blacklog in unpaid pensions and wages that has driven millions of Russians deeper into poverty and undermined support for his government's reforms.
The Kremlin blames tax-dodgers for the late payments.
Alexiy, 67, decried the growing gap between a wealthy few who have benefited from Russia's economic reforms and a majority that must struggle to make ends meet.
Many ordinary Russians, including professionals such as teachers and doctors, have seen a big drop in their living standards as Russia moves from state socialism to a market economy.

"At all times the Church has been and remains on the side of the weak and the unfortunate...it cannot fail to raise its voice in defence of those who find themselves on the brink of life and death as a result of tragic impoverishment," he said.
Later on Monday the white-bearded patriarch, dressed in flowing robes and surrounded by icons, wished his compatriots a happy and peaceful new year in a television broadcast.
The break-up of the Soviet Union in 1991 freed Alexiy from the tough state ideological control that hampered his predecessors in communist times.

He has tried to carve out a broader role for the church amid Russia's post-communist social turmoil and the country's secular leaders have tried to exploit its spiritual authority and rich traditions to bolster their own power.

Yeltsin, who attends key religious ceremonies served by Alexiy in Moscow's Bogoyavlensky cathedral, sent a seasonal message to the patriarch on Monday, the Kremlin's press spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky told reporters.

"The Russian Orthodox Church has made and continues to make a major contribution to the affirmation of high ideals of spirituality and the achievement of unity and concord among the peoples of the Russian state," Yastrzhembsky quoted Yeltsin's greeting as saying.
Alexiy, whose full title is Patriarch of Moscow and all Russia, assumed his post in 1990. He was recently treated in hospital for pneumonia but appeared in good health on Monday.
Russian television said Alexiy would conduct a Christmas service at Moscow's Cathedral of the Epiphany on Monday night.
